conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks after birth, because the emotional changes can be just as big as the physical ones.  

I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s only ten questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety.  

We’ll take it one question at a time, and we can pause whenever you need. Ready to begin?

1. Over the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt for you?

Honestly? It’s been hard. I can still smile if someone shows me a funny video or if my partner cracks a joke, but the laughter feels kind of… flat, like it doesn’t quite reach me the way it used to. I’ll chuckle, then it fades fast and I’m right back to feeling heavy again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I haven’t really felt that way much at all this week. I can fake a little laugh if I have to, but nothing feels genuinely funny inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a show I liked—but now it’s like, “what’s the point?” I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I know, logically, babies cry, but I still feel like it’s my fault, especially when I can’t settle him right away.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much daily. My heart races over little things—like whether the baby’s breathing when he sleeps, or if I sterilized the bottles long enough. I’ll tell myself it’s irrational, but the worry just hangs there and I can’t shake it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful’s about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to rest, it feels like I’m drowning. I manage to keep everything done, but it’s like I’m barely treading water and waiting for the next wave to hit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights. I lie there with my mind racing—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I might’ve messed up—and it takes forever to drift off. Then I jerk awake an hour or two later, heart pounding, and the cycle starts again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
A couple of times. Once was after a diaper change—he peed on me and I just sat on the floor and sobbed. It wasn’t about the mess; it just felt like one more thing I couldn’t handle.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’ve had a couple of quick flashes—like, “what if I just didn’t wake up?”—but I shake them off right away. I don’t want to die; I just want the pressure to stop. I’ve never made a plan or anything, and I’d never leave my baby.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, 1 week after delivery  
Informant: Self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  
Date: [today]

Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (“bad mom” cognitions)  
- Generalized anxiety, near-daily panic-like episodes (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia directly linked to ruminative worry  
- Frequent feeling “overwhelmed” and “drowning” in routine infant tasks  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan, no intent); denies active desire to die  

Pattern  
Symptoms cluster in depressive (mood, pleasure, guilt, tearfulness) and anxiety domains; functional impairment evident; safety concern noted.

Screening Significance  
Score suggests probable major depressive episode with anxious features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder; monitor for escalation of self-harm thoughts.

Safety Flag  
Any self-harm ideation, even passive, warrants immediate safety assessment and possible crisis intervention.

Next Step  
Recommend expedited clinical evaluation (within 24-48 hr) for formal diagnostic clarification and risk management planning.
